topic.subject: social
topic.title: Power sharing and federalism
topic.scope: Belgium and Sri Lanka, horizontal and vertical sharing, union, state and concurrent lists, decentralisation

nodes.name: Case Studies: Belgium vs Sri Lanka

misconceptions.statement: Democracy means the majority community should decide everything for the country.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the democratic principle of majority rule with the ethical requirement to protect minority rights.
misconceptions.fix: Democracy requires that the majority rules while respecting the identity and rights of minority groups to prevent tyranny.

probe.question: In a democracy, if 80% of people belong to one religion, should they make all laws?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because democracy is the rule of the majority.

misconceptions.root_belief: Majority rule is the only definition of democracy.

misconceptions.statement: Horizontal power sharing means the government is divided into different levels like central and state.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the physical layout of government (levels) with the functional division of power (organs).
misconceptions.fix: Horizontal power sharing refers to the division of power among the legislature, executive, and judiciary at the same level.

probe.question: Which of these is an example of horizontal power sharing?
probe.wrong_answer: The division of power between the Central and State governments.

misconceptions.root_belief: All divisions of power are the same.

misconceptions.statement: The Central government can make laws on any subject it wants.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that because the Central government is 'higher', it has absolute authority over all subjects.
misconceptions.fix: The Constitution explicitly defines the Union, State, and Concurrent lists, limiting the Central government's power to specific subjects.

probe.question: Can the Central government make laws on subjects in the State list?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is the supreme authority in the country.

misconceptions.root_belief: Bigger or higher means more power.

misconceptions.statement: Decentralisation means the state government loses all power to the local government.
misconceptions.why: Students interpret 'transfer of power' as a zero-sum game where one loses what the other gains.
misconceptions.fix: Decentralisation is the transfer of power from central and state governments to local bodies, but the higher levels retain their constitutional authority.

probe.question: What happens to the State government's power after decentralisation?
probe.wrong_answer: It is abolished or becomes powerless.

misconceptions.root_belief: Power is a finite resource that must be lost to be shared.

misconceptions.statement: Belgium solved its ethnic tensions by giving all power to the Dutch-speaking majority.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the majoritarian idea from Sri Lanka and assume the larger group must rule in any country.
misconceptions.fix: Belgium accommodated differences by sharing power. Dutch and French speakers have equal representation in the Central government, and Brussels has a separate government in which both communities have equal representation.

probe.question: How did Belgium deal with the Dutch-French divide, and why did it avoid civil war?
probe.wrong_answer: The Dutch-speaking majority took control of the government and the French speakers accepted it.

misconceptions.root_belief: Stable countries are ruled by their largest group
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.1; classroom error analysis

misconceptions.statement: Power sharing is useful only because it reduces conflict, so it has no value beyond that.
misconceptions.why: Students remember the prudential reasons (avoiding conflict) best because the case studies stress them.
misconceptions.fix: There are two reasons. The prudential reason is that power sharing reduces conflict and brings stability. The moral reason is that power sharing is valuable in itself, because it is the spirit of democracy and lets people have a say in how they are governed.

probe.question: If a country has no social conflict at all, is power sharing still needed? Why?
probe.wrong_answer: No, power sharing is needed only to stop conflict, so without conflict it is not needed.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only practical benefits justify a political arrangement
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.1; teacher observation

misconceptions.statement: Horizontal power sharing means the government shares power with social groups such as religious or linguistic communities.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the horizontal form with the community-based form and with political parties and pressure groups.
misconceptions.fix: Horizontal power sharing is among the organs of government at the same level: legislature, executive and judiciary. Sharing among social groups is a separate form, and sharing among parties, movements and pressure groups is another.

probe.question: Which form of power sharing is the separation of powers among the legislature, executive and judiciary?
probe.wrong_answer: It is power sharing among religious and linguistic communities.

misconceptions.root_belief: Horizontal means spread across social groups
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.1; classroom error analysis

misconceptions.statement: Vertical power sharing is the same as federalism, so any country with a central government and local governments is a federation.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the term federalism as just any division of power between levels.
misconceptions.fix: Vertical power sharing is the division of power among governments at different levels. Federalism is a system with two or more levels of government whose powers are constitutionally guaranteed. In a unitary system, the lower-level governments work under the central one and can be changed by it.

probe.question: A country has a central government and local governments, but the centre can dissolve the local bodies at will. Is it a federation?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has two levels of government sharing power.

misconceptions.root_belief: Any multi-level government counts as federal
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2

misconceptions.statement: Education and forests are on the Union List because they are important for the whole country.
misconceptions.why: Students guess from how important a subject sounds and do not remember which list holds it.
misconceptions.fix: The Union List has national-level subjects such as defence, foreign affairs, banking and currency. The State List has subjects such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation. The Concurrent List has subjects of common interest such as education, forests, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession. Both the Union and State governments can make laws on it, and the Union law prevails in case of a conflict.

probe.question: Which list do education and forests belong to, and who can make laws on them?
probe.wrong_answer: The Union List, so only the Central government can make laws on them.

misconceptions.root_belief: Important subjects always belong to the Centre
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2

misconceptions.statement: Decentralisation was introduced in India only in 1992 when local governments were created.
misconceptions.why: Students link decentralisation only with the 1992 amendment and ignore the earlier federal division of power.
misconceptions.fix: India's Constitution already provided for a two-tier system, the Union and the States, and later a third tier. Local governments existed earlier but had no constitutional status or regular elections. The 1992 amendment made them stronger by making elections regular and giving them constitutional status and reserved seats.

probe.question: What did the 1992 Constitutional amendment change about local government in India?
probe.wrong_answer: It created local government in India for the first time.

misconceptions.root_belief: A reform marks the start of the thing it reformed
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2

misconceptions.statement: Residuary powers in India belong to the State governments because states are closer to the people.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the 'leftover' subjects go to the lower level, as in the example of local administration.
misconceptions.fix: Residuary subjects are those that were not on any list, such as computer software, which did not exist when the Constitution was made. In India these go to the Union government. In some other federations, such as the USA and Australia, they go to the states.

probe.question: Which government can make laws on a new subject, such as computer software, that is on none of the three lists?
probe.wrong_answer: The State governments, because they are closer to the people.

misconceptions.root_belief: Leftover power goes to the lower government
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2

misconceptions.statement: A Panchayati Raj gram panchayat is chosen by the state government, which appoints its sarpanch.
misconceptions.why: Students see local bodies as administrative offices working under state officials and not as elected bodies.
misconceptions.fix: The gram panchayat is the local government in a village or group of villages. Its members are elected by all adult residents who are members of the gram sabha, and the sarpanch is its elected president. The gram sabha meets to approve the budget and review the work of the panchayat.

probe.question: Who chooses the members of the gram panchayat and the sarpanch?

misconceptions.root_belief: Local bodies are appointed, not elected
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2; teacher observation
